what: Terrain radiation shielding at Curiosity's Murray Buttes stop (butte M12), MarsNav model vs RAD

measured.source: Ehresmann et al. 2021, JGR Planets 126, e2021JE006851 (abstract)
measured.albedo_share_source: Guo et al. 2021, GRL 48, e2021GL093912 (abstract): albedo ~19 % of flat-terrain dose

terrain.near: HiRISE 1 m within 1500 m, 5 m within 6000 m
terrain.far: Mount Sharp site 100 m regional DEM (CTX) to 25 km

findings: Geometry from orbit is unresolved at this stop: the HiRISE 1 m DTM gives 9 % of the sky blocked at the reported position but 5 % to 16 % within 24 m of it, because the butte face is a few metres away and is smoothed by the DTM; the published 19 % (seen from the rover itself) is above that range. Orbital terrain therefore under-states shelter right against a cliff, the conservative direction for dose.

Dose formula at the published geometry: a wall 25-60 deg high blocking 19 % of the sky gives -9.9 % to -2.6 % against the reference stops; RAD measured about -4 %, which corresponds to a wall about 30 deg high. Without the butte's own albedo the formula would give -15.1 % to -5.9 %, which overshoots at the same heights.
caveats: The albedo share (19 %) was itself derived by Guo et al. from this butte, so agreement on the dose change is a consistency check of the model, not an independent test; the blocked-sky fraction is an independent check of the terrain geometry.
Measured values are as stated in the papers' abstracts.
RAD is a small instrument on a rover; a suited person is larger, and the rover body itself shields RAD from below.
